title: Episode 74: The Crater of Diamonds: The Only Diamond Mine on Earth Open to the Public
description:
The Crater of Diamonds: The Only Diamond Mine on Earth Open to the Public: How an Arkansas farmer found shiny stones in his turnip patch, sparking a diamond rush in the volcanic soil of Murfreesboro. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the late summer of 1906, in the rolling pine hills of Pike County, Arkansas, an impoverished farmer named John Wesley Huddleston was on his hands and knees clearing weeds from his turnip field. Glancing down into the dark, greenish-black dirt, he spotted two tiny, glittering pebbles that sparkled in the sunlight like glass. When local jewelers confirmed that the stones were genuine, high-grade diamonds, the sleepy hamlet of Murfreesboro was catapulted into the craziest mining stampede east of the Rockies. Over the next half-century, industrial syndicates, international jewel merchants, and eccentric prospectors battled to exploit the subterranean treasure. Today, it remains the only diamond-bearing site on planet Earth where everyday members of the public can dig for treasure and keep whatever gems they find. George brings us the sparkling saga of the Crater of Diamonds.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: TWO PEBBLES IN THE TURNIP PATCH
In nineteen oh-six, John Wesley Huddleston was a hardscrabble, uneducated forty-six-year-old farmer who owned a one-hundred-and-sixty-acre homestead two miles south of Murfreesboro, Arkansas. Locals nicknamed him 'Diamond John' because he spent hours staring at the ground, convinced that the strange, greenish-black volcanic soil on his farm contained hidden mineral wealth. The local community considered him an eccentric dreamer whose farm had been foreclosed upon multiple times. On Saturday morning, August fourth, nineteen oh-six, Huddleston was crawling along the furrows of his turnip patch, hunting for stray hogs. In the dark earth, his eye caught a brilliant glint of light. He reached down and picked up an eight-sided, translucent crystal the size of a pea. Continuing to search the furrow, he discovered a second, slightly smaller crystal. Intrigued, Huddleston took the stones to the local bank in Murfreesboro. Bank cashier Carl Lee scratched the stones against a pane of window glass, which they sliced through effortlessly, and tested them against a corundum grindstone. Lee sent the stones to Charles Stifft, a prominent manufacturing jeweler in Little Rock, who in turn forwarded them to George F. Kunz, the world-renowned chief gemologist for Tiffany and Company in New York. Kunz's telegram stunned Arkansas: the stones were genuine, flawless diamonds of exceptional quality. John Huddleston was a modest subsistence farmer who had lived on the rocky Ouachita foothills for years, frequently enduring good-natured ribbing from neighbors who believed the strange greenish soil in his field was worthless for growing cotton or corn. When local assayer Charles S. Stifft confirmed that Huddleston curious pebbles were genuine gem-quality diamonds, the discovery made front-page headlines across the nation, sparking the first and only commercial diamond rush in American history. Neighbors initially scoffed at Huddleston claims, but when word spread that Tiffany and Company in New York had appraised the specimens as genuine white and yellow diamonds, local farmland prices quadrupled overnight.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CRETACEOUS VOLCANIC PIPE
What John Huddleston had stumbled upon was a geological phenomenon of extreme rarity: a lamproite volcanic diamond pipe. Approximately one hundred million years ago, during the Cretaceous period when dinosaurs roamed North America, a subterranean volcanic explosion originating over one hundred miles deep within the Earth's mantle blasted through the continental crust at supersonic speeds. The immense heat and pressure of the Earth's interior had crystallized pure carbon into diamonds billions of years earlier; the ascending molten magma carried these diamonds skyward, creating an eighty-three-acre funnel-shaped volcanic crater filled with weathered peridotite breccia and kimberlite-related green clay. Over millions of years, the volcano eroded away, leaving a diamond-bearing volcanic core resting directly at the surface. It was the only known in-situ diamond pipe in North America, and one of the rarest geological structures in the world. Geologists determined that three billion years ago, deep subterranean volcanic forces pushed diamond-bearing mantle rock up from eighty miles beneath the Earth's crust through a supersonic Kimberlite pipe, preserving diamonds in an ancient seventy-three-acre volcanic crater. Geologists determined that three billion years ago, deep subterranean volcanic forces pushed diamond-bearing mantle rock up from eighty miles beneath the Earth crust through a supersonic Kimberlite pipe, preserving diamonds in an ancient seventy-three-acre volcanic crater.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MURFREESBORO STAMPEDE
When Little Rock newspapers announced that diamonds had been discovered on an Arkansas farm, pandemonium erupted across the region. Within forty-eight hours, the quiet agricultural village of Murfreesboro was swarmed by thousands of prospectors, geologists, jewel syndicates, and curious tourists arriving on special chartered trains. Hotels, livery stables, and boarding houses overflowed, and tents sprang up across the pastures. John Huddleston, overwhelmed by the crowds trampling his crops and eager to pay off his debts, sold his farm and mineral rights to a Little Rock investment syndicate for thirty-six thousand dollars in cash—a staggering fortune for an impoverished dirt farmer, though it would yield millions for its corporate owners. Armed guards were posted with Winchester rifles along barbed-wire fences surrounding the volcanic crater, as armed security forces patrolled the perimeter to keep midnight claim-jumpers from scooping up diamond-bearing gravel in buckets. Thousands of hopeful prospectors, jewelers, and investors flooded the sleepy town of Murfreesboro by train and wagon, pitching canvas tents along the Little Missouri River and turning the local livery stables and boarding houses into a chaotic frontier boomtown. Armed guards patrolled the perimeter fence day and night with shotguns to deter nocturnal diamond poachers who crept through the creek beds with lanterns and wire strainers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE INDUSTRIAL WARS AND THE MYSTERIOUS FIRES
For the next four decades, the Arkansas diamond field became a battleground of competing corporate syndicates. In nineteen oh-seven, the Arkansas Diamond Company and the Ozark Diamond Mines Corporation erected massive industrial washing plants, bringing in steam shovels, rotary screens, and vibrating grease tables imported from the De Beers diamond mines in Kimberley, South Africa. Diamonds stuck naturally to the animal grease on the shaking tables while waste gravel washed away. Thousands of high-quality industrial and gem-grade diamonds were extracted. But industrial diamond mining in Arkansas was plagued by relentless bad luck, shareholder litigation, and corporate sabotage. Speculation swirled that the powerful De Beers diamond cartel secretly manipulated corporate stock and blocked export financing to prevent American diamond production from challenging their global monopoly on diamond prices. Furthermore, mysterious midnight fires repeatedly burned down multi-million-dollar processing plants on the property, and by the nineteen thirties, industrial operations had collapsed into bankruptcy. Corporate syndicates attempted to mechanize diamond recovery with massive steam shovels, trommels, and grease tables, but mysterious arson fires, equipment breakdowns, and financial panics doomed every commercial mining venture, preserving the field for future public exploration. Speculators from New York, London, and Johannesburg formed competing syndicates to acquire mineral rights, but the peculiar clay soil became a sticky, unmanageable gumbo when wet, clogging industrial processing machinery.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT GEMS OF THE CRATER
Despite industrial failures, the volcanic soil continued to yield some of the most spectacular, historically significant gemstones ever discovered in North America. In nineteen twenty-four, a processing plant worker named Wesley Oley Basham was examining the washing screens when he uncovered the 'Uncle Sam' diamond: a breathtaking, forty point twenty-three-carat white diamond. It remains to this day the largest diamond ever unearthed on the North American continent. Cut in Boston into a flawless twelve point forty-two-carat emerald-cut gem, the Uncle Sam diamond was sold for one hundred and fifty thousand dollars, eventually acquired by prominent private collectors. In nineteen fifty-six, a Dallas woman named Winifred Parker discovered the 'Star of Arkansas,' a stunning fifteen point thirty-three-carat white diamond; and in nineteen seventy-five, local resident W.W. Johnson unearthed the 'Esperanza' diamond, an eight point fifty-two-carat gem cut into a triolette shape valued at over one million dollars. Over seventy-five thousand diamonds have been cataloged from the eighty-three-acre field, ranging in colors from canary yellow to ice white and chocolate brown. Over thirty-three thousand diamonds have been unearthed from the crater's plowed fields, including the remarkable forty-carat Uncle Sam diamond—the largest diamond ever discovered in North America—and the immaculate, flawless three-carat Strawn-Wagner diamond. The discovery of the canary-yellow Esperanza diamond in twenty-fifteen and the four-carat Amarillo Starlight proved that massive, flawless gemstones still lie hidden just inches beneath the plowed furrow lines.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PEOPLE'S DIAMOND MINE
In nineteen fifty-two, an enterprising promoter named Howard Millar converted the property into a commercial tourist attraction, christening it the 'Crater of Diamonds.' For a modest daily admission fee, everyday visitors were invited to bring hand shovels and screen boxes to hunt for gems, keeping whatever diamonds they found. Recognizing that the site was a priceless natural treasure that belonged to all citizens, the State of Arkansas purchased the entire eight-hundred-and-eighty-acre property in nineteen seventy-two for seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars, establishing Crater of Diamonds State Park under the stewardship of the Arkansas Department of Parks, Heritage, and Tourism. It became the only diamond-producing site on the planet operated as a public park, embodying an egalitarian frontier philosophy: here, any child or amateur prospector could experience the thrill of striking treasure in the red clay. The Arkansas Department of Parks and Tourism acquired the property in nineteen seventy-two, establishing a unique state park where visitors of all ages can rent shovels and box screens, retaining full legal ownership of every gemstone they unearth from the soil. Park rangers plow the thirty-seven-acre search field regularly with heavy tractors, exposing fresh layers of diamond-bearing volcanic soil and allowing natural rainfall to wash away light gravel and reveal sparkling crystals. Geologists and gemologists from prestigious research institutes frequently visit the state park, studying the rare lamproite rock matrix and marveling at the unique geological anomaly that preserved these ancient diamonds.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LIVING FIELD OF DREAMS
Today, Crater of Diamonds State Park attracts over one hundred thousand treasure hunters every year from across the United States and foreign nations. The thirty-seven-acre plowed volcanic field is plowed regularly by state park tractors to loosen the soil and allow heavy rains to wash away clay, exposing sparkling gems to the sunlight. On average, visitors find one to two genuine diamonds every single day, along with amethyst, garnet, jasper, and agate. Park rangers operate a dedicated diamond identification laboratory, verifying each discovery, weighing the stones on precision gem scales, and issuing official certificates of authenticity. The Crater of Diamonds remains an enchanting symbol of American possibility: a magical landscape where an impoverished farmer searching for stray hogs in a turnip field stumbled upon the secrets of the mantle, proving that wonders still lie waiting just beneath our feet. Every year, hundreds of sparkling diamonds are discovered by amateur park visitors wandering the plowed volcanic soil after heavy rains, keeping alive the timeless thrill of frontier treasure hunting in the scenic pine hills of southwest Arkansas. Visitors from every corner of the world gather in the Arkansas sunshine with buckets, trowels, and screens, bound by the universal joy of discovery and the thrilling possibility of finding a priceless treasure in the earth. The Crater of Diamonds stands as a beloved American institution where families, amateur rockhounds, and curiosity seekers share in the pure excitement of unearthing nature most glittering creations with their own hands.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Crater of Diamonds is an extraordinary testament to the natural wonders of our planet and the timeless allure of discovery. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week for another thrilling journey through the most fascinating stories of our world.
